title: Synthetic data and model collapse
summary: Why models trained on their own outputs lose the tails and collapse, how replacing, accumulating and mixing data change the math, and how verification and diversity make synthetic data work at scale.
outcomes: Explain why finite resampling erases rare events and why a fully synthetic loop is absorbed into a point mass
Compute the per-generation chance of losing a token and the variance drift of a Gaussian fit-and-resample loop
Explain how temperature, top-k and top-p cut tails and why that makes scaling plateau
Simulate collapse in NumPy and measure diversity with distinct-n, self-ROUGE-L, embedding spread and rare coverage
Compare replace, accumulate and fixed-share mixing, compute their test error, and name the collapse definition each uses
Compute the accuracy of a verifier-filtered synthetic set and the breakdown point beyond which training on it fails
Design a synthetic data pipeline with outside filtering, injected diversity and real-data anchoring

lessons.title: Why resampling your own outputs erases rare events

blocks.md: From the training course you know an LLM is pretrained on a huge web scrape, then fine-tuned. Two things now put model-written text into that pipeline. Labs generate **synthetic data** on purpose (instructions, reasoning traces, textbook-style explanations), and the web itself fills with model output that a future scrape will collect. Either way, a model can end up learning from the outputs of earlier models.

Shumailov et al. asked what happens when this repeats: model 1 is trained on real data, model 2 on samples from model 1, model 3 on samples from model 2, and so on. The work first appeared on arXiv in 2023 as *The Curse of Recursion* and was published in *Nature* in 2024; later lessons cite both versions. They named the result **model collapse**: a degenerative process where each generation's output pollutes the next generation's training set, so models slowly forget the true distribution. They separate **early collapse**, where the rare events in the tails of the distribution vanish, from **late collapse**, where the model converges to a distribution with little resemblance to the original, often with much smaller variance.

Start with the simplest possible model: no neural network at all. The "model" is a histogram over 6 tokens, fitted by counting. Each generation draws $M = 20$ samples from the current histogram, counts them, and the new counts divided by 20 become the next model. Fitting is perfect here; the only error is that 20 samples are a finite sample. The true probabilities are 0.40, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10, 0.07 and 0.03.

blocks.prompt: The rarest token, *aardvark*, has probability 0.03. With 20 samples per generation, what is the chance that generation 1 contains no aardvark at all?
blocks.reveal: About **54%**. The chance one sample misses it is 0.97, so all 20 miss with probability $0.97^{20} = 0.544$. Its expected count is $20 \times 0.03 = 0.6$, less than one occurrence. Once a count is zero, the fitted histogram gives that token probability zero, so it can never be sampled again.

blocks.tex: P(\text{token lost in one generation}) = (1-q)^M, \qquad \mathbb{E}[\text{count}] = Mq
blocks.caption: q is the token's current probability, M the samples per generation. Any token with q below 1/M is expected to appear less than once.

scenes.caption: Generation 0 is the real distribution. aardvark (0.03) and mat (0.07) both have expected counts below 1.5 in a sample of 20.

blocks.md: Why must every run end in a spike? The sequence of histograms is a **Markov chain**: the next histogram depends only on the current one. A histogram with all mass on one token reproduces itself exactly, so it is an **absorbing state**, and a chain that can reach an absorbing state from anywhere is absorbed with probability 1. Shumailov et al. also note the chance of ending on a given token equals its original probability. Here is why. A token with probability $q$ has expected count $Mq$ in the next sample, so its expected refitted probability is $Mq/M = q$: on average it does not move. A quantity whose expected next value equals its current value is called a **martingale**, so its expected value stays $q$ forever. At the end it is 1 if the token won and 0 if it lost, so the chance that it wins must be $q$. In 20,000 simulated runs of this example, *the* won 39.6% of the time (true 0.40) and *aardvark* 2.9% (true 0.03), and the mean time to a single spike was 32.5 generations.
In a closed loop that only ever trains on its own samples, information can be lost but never regained. Rare events go first, because their expected count in a finite sample is below one.

Model collapse is not caused by a bad model or a bug. In this example fitting is exact. The finite sample alone, which Shumailov et al. call **statistical approximation error**, is enough to drive the process.

blocks.question: A token's fitted probability hits exactly 0 at generation 4 of this fully synthetic loop. What is the chance it reappears at generation 50?
options: About its original probability, because errors average out over generations
Small but positive, because sampling is random
Zero, because a token with probability 0 is never sampled and refitting cannot invent it
About 1/M, because each generation draws M fresh samples
blocks.explain: The histogram model can only assign mass to tokens it has seen. Once a count is zero the token has probability zero, so no later sample contains it. Only an outside source of real data could bring it back.

blocks.question: In the absorbing chain above, cat starts at probability 0.25. Over many independent runs, roughly how often does cat end up as the sole surviving token?
options: About 25% of runs
Never, only the most common token can win
About 1/6 of runs, since all tokens are symmetric
About 50%, since it is the second most likely
blocks.explain: The fitted probability is a martingale: its expected value never changes, so the chance of absorbing at a token equals its starting probability. The 20,000-run simulation gave 25.5% for cat.

lessons.title: The Gaussian loop: unbiased fits that still shrink to a point

blocks.md: The histogram had discrete tokens. Real models fit continuous distributions, so take the next simplest case. The data are a one-dimensional Gaussian with mean $\mu = 0$ and standard deviation $\sigma = 1$, written $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ (the second number is the variance $\sigma^2$); a Gaussian with mean 0 and variance 1 is called a **standard normal**. Each generation draws $M$ samples from the current model, then fits a new Gaussian using the **unbiased** sample mean and sample variance (dividing by $M-1$). Unbiased means the estimate is right on average over many samples. Dividing the squared deviations by $M$ would come out too small on average, because they are measured from the sample's own mean, which sits closer to the samples than the true mean does; dividing by $M-1$ corrects exactly for that. The next generation samples from that fit.

blocks.caption: The recursive fitting process from Shumailov et al. (Eq. 1 and 2 of the arXiv version). In words: the new mean is the average of the M samples, the new variance is their squared distance from it summed and divided by M minus 1, and the next generation samples from that Gaussian.

blocks.title: Fit, sample, refit: one seeded run with M = 10
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
mu, sigma, M = 0.0, 1.0, 10
for gen in range(1, 101):
    x = rng.normal(mu, sigma, M)  # sample from current model
    mu = x.mean()                 # refit the mean
    sigma = x.std(ddof=1)         # refit with unbiased variance
print(round(mu, 3), round(sigma, 4))

scenes.caption: Generation 0 is the true distribution: mean 0, standard deviation 1. Only 10 samples are drawn per generation.
After one fit the estimate is already off: the 10 samples happened to be bunched together, so sigma dropped to 0.781.
Generation 10: sigma is 0.430. Each fit starts from the previous fit, not from the truth, so errors compound instead of cancelling.
Generation 50: sigma is 0.104 and the mean has wandered to -0.374. The model now covers only a sliver around a wrong center.
Generation 100: sigma is about 0.0001. Late collapse: a near point mass at a random location. The mean has stopped moving because the steps scale with sigma.

blocks.prompt: The variance estimator is unbiased: averaged over runs, $\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2_{n+1}] = \sigma^2_n$, so $\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2_n] = 1$ at every generation. How can almost every run still collapse toward zero?
blocks.reveal: Because the average is carried by rare runs. The product of many random factors with mean 1 is typically far below 1: each generation multiplies $\sigma^2$ by a factor $S$ whose mean is 1 but whose log has a negative mean. In 200,000 simulated runs with $M = 10$, at generation 10 the average $\sigma^2$ was 1.006, yet the median $\sigma$ was 0.573 and 43% of runs had $\sigma < 0.5$. A few runs with huge variance hold the average up while the typical run shrinks.

blocks.md: Write the update as $\sigma^2_{n+1} = \sigma^2_n S_n$, where $S_n = \chi^2_{M-1}/(M-1)$ is an independent random factor with mean exactly 1 (a chi-squared variable with $M-1$ degrees of freedom is a sum of the squares of $M-1$ independent standard normals, divided here by its mean). The count is $M-1$ rather than $M$ because fitting the mean from the same samples uses up one of them.

Taking logs turns the product into a sum: $\ln \sigma^2_n = \sum_i \ln S_i$. **Jensen's inequality** says that for a curved-down function like log, the average of the log is below the log of the average: if $S$ is 0.5 or 1.5 with equal chance, its mean is 1 and $\ln 1 = 0$, but the mean of the logs is $-0.144$, half of $-0.693 + 0.405$. So $\mathbb{E}[\ln S] < \ln \mathbb{E}[S] = 0$, and the log-variance is a random walk whose average step, its **drift**, is negative. The law of large numbers says a sum of $n$ independent steps is close to $n$ times their mean, so it drives the log-variance to minus infinity.

How big is the drift? For a chi-squared variable with $k$ degrees of freedom the average log is known exactly: $\psi(k/2) + \ln 2$, where $\psi$, the **digamma function**, is the derivative of the log of the gamma function (the gamma function extends the factorial to non-integers). Dividing by $k = M-1$ subtracts $\ln k$, which gives the drift $\psi(k/2) - \ln(k/2)$. For large $x$, $\psi(x)$ is about $\ln x$ minus one over twice $x$, so the drift is about $-1/(M-1)$. After $n$ generations $\ln \sigma^2_n \approx -n/(M-1)$, and $\ln \sigma_n$ is half of that, so $\sigma$ halves each time the summed drift falls by $2 \ln 2$: every $2 \ln 2 / 0.1152 \approx 12$ generations for $M = 10$.

blocks.caption: psi is the digamma function. In words: the average log of S is about minus 1 over M minus 1, so sigma decays exponentially. For M = 10 the exact drift is -0.1152 per generation (the approximation gives -0.1111), so a typical sigma halves about every 12 generations.

scenes.caption: M = 10: sigma halves about every 12 generations and is effectively zero by generation 100. Simplified: this is the drift approximation, not one run.
M = 100: the exact halving time is about 137 generations. Collapse is slower, not prevented.

M = 1000: about 1384 generations per halving. Larger samples only stretch the timeline; Theorem 3.1 of the Nature paper says sigma still goes to 0 almost surely, that is, with probability 1, for any fixed M.

blocks.md: Shumailov et al. also measure the distance from the truth with the **Wasserstein-2 distance**. Picture moving probability mass to turn one distribution into the other, paying the squared distance each bit of mass moves: $W_2^2$ is the smallest possible average cost, and $W_2$ its square root. For two one-dimensional Gaussians it has a closed form, $W_2^2 = (\mu_n - \mu)^2 + (\sigma_n - \sigma)^2$. To first order in $1/M$ (keeping terms of size $1/M$ and dropping smaller ones like $1/M^2$), after $n$ fits its expected value grows linearly: $\mathbb{E}[W_2^2] \approx 1.5\,\sigma^2 n/M$ (our simulation with $M = 10$ gave 1.49 at $n = 10$, against 1.5 predicted).

The 1.5 has two parts: the fitted mean takes a random step of variance $\sigma^2/M$ each generation, adding up to $n\sigma^2/M$, and the fitted standard deviation takes a step of variance about $\sigma^2/(2M)$, adding $n\sigma^2/(2M)$. That mean step keeps an expected squared size of $\sigma^2/M$ in every generation (rare high-variance runs keep it up), so the expected error keeps growing even though a typical run's mean freezes as its sigma shrinks, and the paper's Theorem 3.1 states that $\mathbb{E}[W_2^2] \to \infty$ while $\sigma^2_n \to 0$ almost surely (the paper writes the variance as $\Sigma_n$, the covariance matrix in higher dimensions).

Keeping the error bounded needs sample sizes that grow **superlinearly**, faster than in proportion to the generation count. Here is why. If generation $i$ draws $M_i$ samples, the arXiv version of the paper gives, to first order, $\mathbb{E}[W_2^2] \approx \tfrac{3}{2}\sigma^2 (1/M_0 + 1/M_1 + \dots + 1/M_n)$: every generation adds its own sampling variance, so the error stays bounded only if that sum converges. A constant $M$ adds the same amount every generation, so the sum grows linearly. Growing the sample in proportion to the generation, $M_i \propto i$, gives the harmonic series $1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + \dots$, which still grows without limit (like $\ln n$). Only faster growth, such as $M_i \propto i^2$ (the authors suggest "perhaps quadratically"), makes the sum converge.

The Nature version lists three error sources that compound over generations: **statistical approximation error** (finite samples, the primary cause), **functional expressivity error** (the model family cannot represent the true distribution, such as fitting one Gaussian to two bumps), and **functional approximation error** (limits of the learning procedure itself, such as biases of SGD or the choice of objective). Real neural networks have all three.
Sampling error makes each generation's fit a random step, and steps that multiply variance by a mean-one factor still shrink it in the typical run. Unbiased estimation does not save a closed loop.

blocks.question: A team fixes collapse in this Gaussian loop by raising M from 10 to 100 samples per generation, keeping everything else the same. What actually happens?
options: Collapse stops, because the estimator becomes accurate enough
Collapse is slowed roughly tenfold (halving time about 12 to about 137 generations) but still happens
Collapse speeds up, because more samples overfit
Nothing changes, because the estimator was already unbiased
blocks.explain: The drift of log-variance is about -1/(M-1) per generation, so a 10x larger sample makes it about 10x smaller. It never reaches zero for finite M, so sigma still tends to 0. Only fresh real data or growing sample sizes change the outcome.

blocks.question: Which statement about the M = 10 loop is correct?
options: The expected variance falls each generation, so the estimator is biased
The typical variance stays near 1, but the expected variance collapses
The expected variance stays at 1, but the typical (median) run collapses toward 0
Both the expected and typical variance stay near 1
blocks.explain: Unbiasedness makes the variance a martingale, so its expectation is 1 forever. The median follows the drift of the log and collapses. A heavy right tail of rare runs keeps the mean at 1.

lessons.title: Language models: decoding cuts the tail, scaling stalls

blocks.md: Does any of this show up in real LLMs? Shumailov et al. fine-tuned Meta's OPT-125m (OPT stands for Open Pre-trained Transformer; this one has 125 million parameters) on the wikitext2 dataset (about 2 million training tokens from Wikipedia articles that editors rated Good or Featured), then generated a full synthetic copy of the training set: for every 64-token block of real text, the model continued with 64 tokens using 5-way **beam search**: a decoder that keeps the 5 most probable partial continuations, extends each by one token, and again keeps the 5 with the highest total log-probability, so it favors the most likely text. The next generation was fine-tuned on that synthetic set, and so on. The real-data model reached a mean perplexity of 34 on the wikitext2 test set, down from a zero-shot 115 (zero-shot: the pretrained model before any fine-tuning on wikitext2). Recall from the training course that perplexity is e raised to the average per-token loss, roughly how many tokens the model is choosing among, so lower is better.

Two settings were compared. With no original data kept and 5 epochs per generation, performance degraded over generations. With 10 epochs and a random 10% of the original data kept in every generation, degradation was only minor. Scored by the original model (the perplexity it assigns to each generated sequence), later generations produced more of the sequences it already found likely, and also a long tail of strange sequences it would never produce. By generation 9 a prompt about church towers produced a list of jackrabbits with differently colored tails.

Language models have an extra way to lose tails that the Gaussian toy lacked: **decoding**. To get fluent synthetic text, practitioners rarely sample from the raw next-token distribution. They use **temperature** $\tau < 1$ (divide logits by $\tau$ before softmax), **top-k** (keep only the $k$ most likely tokens) or **top-p** (keep the smallest set of tokens whose mass reaches $p$). Each one deliberately moves probability away from rare tokens. Beam search, used in the OPT experiment above, sits at the extreme of this picture: it hunts for the most probable continuations, and with a single beam it is greedy decoding, the zero-temperature limit, so its synthetic text under-represents the tail even more than sampling would. Call the model that writes the synthetic data the **teacher** and the model trained on it the **student**.

blocks.title: One next-token distribution under common decoding settings

scenes.caption: A Zipf-like distribution over 8 tokens: probability proportional to 1/rank, the pattern linguist George Zipf found in word frequencies. Ranks 5 to 8 hold 23.3% of the mass.
Temperature 0.7: logits divided by 0.7 sharpen the distribution. Ranks 5 to 8 now hold 14.5%.
Temperature 0.5: the tail holds 6.8%. The tail is narrowed, not removed, but rare tokens will appear far less often.
Top-p 0.8 keeps ranks 1 to 5 (cumulative mass 0.84) and renormalizes. Ranks 6 to 8 get exactly zero: they can never appear in the synthetic data.
Top-k 4: only 4 tokens survive. A student model trained on this output has no evidence that ranks 5 to 8 exist.

blocks.md: Dohmatob et al. (*A Tale of Tails*) turn this into a scaling-law statement. Suppose items (facts, skills, token patterns) occur with Zipf frequencies $p_i \propto i^{-\beta}$ with $\beta > 1$ (which keeps the total probability finite), and a model simply memorizes every item it has seen (the "Hutter LLM", after Marcus Hutter, who analyzed this memorizing model's learning curves in 2021). Its test error is the chance that a fresh item is one it has never seen.

Trained on $T$ real samples, its error falls as $T^{-(\beta-1)/\beta}$. Here is where that comes from: item $i$ has likely been seen once its expected count $T p_i$ reaches about 1, that is for ranks up to about $T^{1/\beta}$, and the unseen items beyond that rank hold mass about $(T^{1/\beta})^{-(\beta-1)} = T^{-(\beta-1)/\beta}$. If the training data come from a generator whose tail is cut at rank $k$, items beyond $k$ are never seen, however much data you generate. Their mass, about $k^{-(\beta-1)}$, is a floor under the error, and the two terms meet when $T^{1/\beta} = k$, that is $T \approx k^\beta$.

blocks.caption: The unseen mass is a sum over ranks beyond K, close to the integral. Check at beta = 2, T = 10^4: K = 100, integral 0.01, exact sum 0.00995. Dividing by the total of all i^-2 (pi^2/6) to get probabilities gives 0.00605, the plateau in the figure below.

Theorem 2.1 of A Tale of Tails (constants dropped). In words: test error is on the order of T to the minus (beta minus 1) over beta, plus k to the minus (beta minus 1). Once T is larger than about k to the power beta, more synthetic samples stop helping: the error plateaus.

blocks.title: Test error of a memorizing model, real versus tail-cut data (beta = 2)

scenes.caption: Real data: error falls by sqrt(10) per 10x data (exact values 0.0069 at T = 10^4, 0.00069 at 10^6). Simplified: curves follow the shape of Theorem 2.1, fitted to an exact computation over 10 million Zipf items.
Cut at k = 100: the error stalls at 0.00605, exactly the real probability mass beyond rank 100. From T = 10^6 to 10^7 it does not move.
Cut at k = 1000: the plateau drops tenfold and starts later (k squared is 10^6 here). A wider generator tail buys more useful scaling, never unlimited.

blocks.md: Fluency is not coverage. Low temperature and truncation make each synthetic sample look better, and that is exactly why they remove the rare cases a student model needs. The MAD paper (Alemohammad et al., *Self-Consuming Generative Models Go MAD*, for Model Autophagy Disorder, by analogy with mad cow disease) finds the same tradeoff for images: biased sampling such as truncation keeps quality longer but loses diversity faster.

blocks.question: You generate 10x more synthetic training text from the same teacher with top-p 0.9. Under the tail-cutting model, when does this stop improving the student?
options: Never: error keeps falling as a power law in T
Once T exceeds roughly k to the power beta, where k is the effective tail cut; after that error plateaus at the missing tail mass
Immediately: synthetic data never helps
Only when the teacher's perplexity exceeds the student's
blocks.explain: Data from a tail-cut generator only teaches the head of the distribution. Once the student has learned the head, the remaining error is the mass of the items it never sees, and more samples from the same generator cannot reveal them.

blocks.question: In the OPT-125m experiment, which change to the loop gave only minor degradation over generations?
options: Using beam search instead of sampling
Training for fewer epochs
Keeping a random 10% of the original real data in every generation
Generating a synthetic dataset twice as large
blocks.explain: Mixing real data back in each generation re-anchors the model to the true distribution. The paper reports only minor degradation in that setting, versus clear degradation with no original data.

lessons.title: Reproduce collapse yourself: simulate the loops, measure diversity

blocks.md: Lessons 1 and 2 derived collapse on paper. Here you run it: a few short NumPy scripts that finish in seconds on a laptop CPU. Start with the histogram loop of lesson 1 exactly as stated there: six tokens with probabilities 0.40 to 0.03, $M = 20$ samples per generation, refit by counting. The script runs it 2,000 times, records how many tokens are still alive at a few checkpoints, how long each run takes to reach a single spike, and which token wins.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

q = np.array([0.40, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10, 0.07, 0.03])
H = -(q * np.log(q)).sum()          # entropy in nats
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

def run(M, checkpoints=(1, 5, 10, 20)):
    p, gen, alive = q.copy(), 0, {}
    while p.max() < 1:
        p = rng.multinomial(M, p) / M   # sample M, refit by counting
        gen += 1
        if gen in checkpoints:
            alive[gen] = (p > 0).sum()
    for c in checkpoints:               # absorbed early: 1 token left
        alive.setdefault(c, 1)
    return gen, p.argmax(), alive

for M in (20, 40):
    runs = [run(M) for _ in range(2000)]
    T = np.mean([r[0] for r in runs])
    wins = np.bincount([r[1] for r in runs], minlength=6) / 2000
    print(f"M={M}: mean generations to a spike {T:.1f} (M*H = {M*H:.1f})")
    print("  share of runs won:", np.round(wins, 3))
    for c in (1, 5, 10, 20):
        print(f"  tokens alive at gen {c}: {np.mean([r[2][c] for r in runs]):.2f}")

(*Model Collapse Does Not Mean What You Think*) note that in this histogram model the expected number of fitting iterations before total collapse is proportional to the sample size times the **entropy** of the starting distribution, $H = -\sum q \ln q$ (the average surprise, in nats; 1.52 here). $M H$ is 30.4 and 60.8, close to the simulated times. Total collapse is slow when samples are large, but the tail tokens still go first.

blocks.md: Now the Gaussian loop of lesson 2, vectorized over 2,000 runs at once. The extra argument `rho` is a switch for mixing in real data: a fraction $\rho$ of each generation's sample is drawn fresh from the true $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ instead of from the current fit.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def loop(M, gens, rho=0.0, runs=2000, seed=0):
    """Median sigma per generation. rho = share of each sample that is real."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    mu = np.zeros(runs); sd = np.ones(runs)
    n_real = int(round(rho * M))
    med = []
    for g in range(gens):
        syn = rng.normal(mu[:, None], sd[:, None], (runs, M - n_real))
        real = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, (runs, n_real))   # fresh true data
        x = np.concatenate([syn, real], axis=1)
        mu, sd = x.mean(1), x.std(1, ddof=1)
        med.append(np.median(sd))
    return np.array(med)

for M in (10, 100):
    med = loop(M, 500)
    for n in (10, 50, 100, 500):
        pred = np.exp(-n / (2 * (M - 1)))
        print(f"M={M:3d} gen {n:3d}: median sigma {med[n-1]:.4f}  drift law {pred:.4f}")

for rho in (0.0, 0.1, 0.3):
    med = loop(10, 500, rho)
    print(f"M=10 rho={rho}: median sigma at gen 50 {med[49]:.3f}, gen 500 {med[499]:.3f}")

blocks.md: The simulated medians track $\exp(-n/(2(M-1)))$ closely. The one visible gap, 0.0032 against 0.0039 at generation 100 for $M = 10$, is the approximation: the exact drift from lesson 2, $-0.1152$ per generation, gives $\exp(-100 \times 0.1152 / 2) = 0.0032$. The mixing switch changes the outcome, not just the speed. With $\rho = 0.1$, a single real sample out of 10 per generation, median sigma sits at 0.90 to 0.93 instead of falling to zero; with $\rho = 0.3$ it sits near 0.96. Each generation the fit still shrinks a little, but the real samples pull it back toward the truth, and the two effects balance at a level slightly below 1.

Back to M = 10, but 1 of the 10 samples in every generation is fresh real data (rho = 0.1). Median sigma no longer decays: it holds near 0.93 out to generation 500.

blocks.md: A closed loop collapses at a rate set by the sample size, and you can measure that rate. A small but steady stream of real data turns the downward drift into a stable level.

In a real pipeline you cannot compute the sigma of the true distribution, so you measure the generated set itself. An **n-gram** is a run of $n$ consecutive words. Four common measurements:

1. **distinct-n** (Li et al. 2016): the number of distinct n-grams divided by the total number of generated words. Low means repetitive.
2. **Self-BLEU** (from the Texygen benchmark, Zhu et al. 2018): score each generated sentence with BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy, a machine-translation metric), an n-gram overlap score, using all the other sentences as references, then average. Higher means less diverse. Self-ROUGE-L does the same with ROUGE-L.
3. **Embedding spread**: the mean pairwise cosine distance between sentence embeddings (1 minus the cosine of the angle between two vectors).
4. **Rare-slice coverage**: how much of the rare part of a held-out real set appears in, or is handled well after training on, the synthetic set.

ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) is a family of text-overlap scores; the L variant scores the longest common subsequence of words, the longest run of words two texts share in the same order, possibly with gaps. As an F1 score it is $2 \times \text{LCS} / (\text{len}_a + \text{len}_b)$, from 0 for nothing shared to 1 for identical. To have something to measure, the next script builds a tiny language model: a **bigram model**, which predicts the next word from counts of which word followed which in 8 training sentences. It samples 5 sentences at temperature 1.0 and 5 at temperature 0.3. Save it as `bigram.py`: the metrics script after it imports the two sets from that file. Temperature works as in lesson 3: raising each count to the power $1/\tau$ and renormalizing is the same as dividing the log-counts by $\tau$ before a softmax.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

corpus = """the cat sat on the mat
the cat ate the fish
the dog sat on the rug
the dog chased the cat
a bird sang on the roof
the old fox slept under the bridge
the cat sat by the door
a child fed the hungry goat""".split("\n")

nxt = defaultdict(Counter)                 # bigram counts
for s in corpus:
    w = ["<s>"] + s.split() + ["</s>"]
    for a, b in zip(w, w[1:]):
        nxt[a][b] += 1

def sample(temp, rng):
    out, w = [], "<s>"
    while len(out) < 12:
        words = list(nxt[w]); c = np.array([nxt[w][x] for x in words], float)
        p = c ** (1 / temp); p /= p.sum()   # temperature on log-counts
        w = words[rng.choice(len(words), p=p)]
        if w == "</s>": break
        out.append(w)
    return " ".join(out)

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
sets = {t: [sample(t, rng) for _ in range(5)] for t in (1.0, 0.3)}
for t, ss in sets.items():
    print(f"temperature {t}:"); [print("  ", s) for s in ss]

blocks.md: Three of these metrics only look inside the generated set: a generator can be varied in phrasing while missing whole topics. Only rare-slice coverage compares against real data, so keep a held-out real set. Also compare sets of equal size and length; distinct-n falls as texts get longer even with no loss of diversity, and 5-sentence sets like these are noisy.

blocks.question: Over five rounds of a synthetic data loop, distinct-2 of the generated set stays near 0.7, but coverage of the rare slice of a held-out real set falls from 0.5 to 0.2. What is the best reading?
options: The generator is fine: distinct-2 is stable, so diversity is preserved
The held-out real set is too small to trust, so ignore it
Diversity is improving, because rare-slice coverage is supposed to fall as quality rises
The phrasing stays varied but rare content is disappearing: the early-collapse signature of losing the tails
blocks.explain: distinct-n measures variety inside the generated set, not whether it still covers the real distribution. Falling rare-slice coverage is exactly the tail loss of lessons 1 and 3, which internal metrics can miss.

blocks.question: In the Gaussian loop with M = 10, you replace 1 of the 10 synthetic samples in every generation with a fresh sample from the true distribution. What does the median sigma do over 500 generations?
options: It settles at a stable level a little below 1 (about 0.93 in the simulation)
It still decays to zero, only about 10% more slowly
It returns exactly to 1, because real data remove all error
It grows above 1, because real and synthetic samples disagree
blocks.explain: The real samples pull each fit back toward the truth while resampling still shrinks it a little, so the two balance. With rho = 0.1 the simulated median was 0.899 at generation 50 and 0.933 at generation 500, against 0.000 with no real data.

lessons.title: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded

blocks.md: Every loop so far **replaced** the training set each generation: model n saw only model n-1's samples. Gerstgrasser et al. argued that is not how real corpora evolve. Meta's open Llama models 1, 2 and 3 were trained on 1.4, 2 and 15 trillion tokens; data **accumulate**, and synthetic text would be added to, not swapped for, the human text already collected. Alemohammad et al. (the MAD paper) distinguish three loops by how real data enter.

scenes.caption: Fully synthetic loop: after generation 1, each training set is only model output. This is the setting of lessons 1 and 2, and it degrades.
Synthetic augmentation loop: a fixed real set stays in the mix. In MAD's image experiments this only delayed degradation.
Fresh data loop: new real data arrive every generation, as when re-scraping the web. MAD finds quality and diversity hold with enough fresh real data.

blocks.md: Gerstgrasser et al. studied the accumulate setting in a model simple enough to solve exactly: linear regression. Real data are $y = x \cdot w^* + \epsilon$, where $x$ holds $d$ input features, $w^*$ is the true weight vector, and $\epsilon$ is random label noise with variance $\sigma^2$ (a new use of sigma: here it is the noise, not the spread of the data). Each iteration fits **ordinary least squares** (OLS: the weights that minimize the summed squared error on the current labels), then relabels the same $T$ inputs using the fitted weights plus fresh noise. Under **replace**, the next fit uses only the newest labels. Under **accumulate**, it uses all labels generated so far, including the original real ones.

How large is the error of one fit? Test error here is the expected squared gap between the fitted model's predictions and the true $x \cdot w^*$ on new inputs. With **isotropic** features (independent standard normal features, the same spread in every direction), one OLS fit on $T$ noisy labels has test error $\sigma^2 d/(T-d-1)$: more noise or more weights to estimate raise it, more samples lower it. Where does $T-d-1$ come from? OLS computes $\hat w = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y$, where $X$ is the $T \times d$ matrix of inputs, so label noise reaches the weights through the inverse of $X^\top X$. The test error is $\sigma^2$ times the average trace (sum of diagonal entries) of that inverse, and for Gaussian inputs that average is exactly $d/(T-d-1)$ (Lemma 3 of Gerstgrasser et al.).

With one feature ($d = 1$), $X^\top X$ is a sum of $T$ squared standard normals, and the average of one over such a sum is $1/(T-2) = 1/(T-d-1)$. The error rises sharply as $T$ approaches $d$ because some direction in feature space is then barely sampled: $X^\top X$ has a tiny eigenvalue there, and inverting it amplifies the noise along that direction. In a simulation with $d = 10$, the median smallest eigenvalue of $X^\top X$ was 53 at $T = 100$, 2.7 at $T = 20$ and 0.30 at $T = 12$; the average trace of the inverse was 0.112, 1.11 and 9.8 (formula: 0.112, 1.11, 10). The formula needs $T - d - 1 > 0$, that is at least $d+2$ samples. After $n$ iterations, replace multiplies the one-fit error by $n$, while accumulate multiplies it by $1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + \dots + 1/n^2$.

blocks.tex: E^{\text{replace}}_{\text{test}} = \frac{\sigma^2 d}{T-d-1}\, n, \qquad E^{\text{accum}}_{\text{test}} = \frac{\sigma^2 d}{T-d-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{i^2} \le \frac{\sigma^2 d}{T-d-1} \cdot \frac{\pi^2}{6}
blocks.caption: Test error after n iterations with isotropic features and T at least d + 2 (the replace result is due to Dohmatob, Feng and Kempe, Model Collapse Demystified, as restated in Eq. 4 of Gerstgrasser et al.; the accumulate bound is their Theorem 2).

blocks.md: Why $1/i^2$? Theorem 1 of Gerstgrasser et al. writes the accumulated fit directly in terms of the noise vectors; the replace fit unrolls the same way. Each iteration $i$ relabels the inputs and adds a fresh noise vector $E_i$ (one noise value per sample). Under replace, each fit inherits the previous one in full, so every $E_i$ stays in the weights with weight 1. Under accumulate, iteration $i$'s labels are one of $i$ label sets in the training data, so $E_i$ enters with weight $1/i$; later label sets are generated from fits that already contain it at that weight, so it stays at $1/i$.

blocks.tex: \hat w^{\text{replace}}_n = w^* + X^{\dagger} \sum_{i=1}^{n} E_i, \qquad \hat w^{\text{accum}}_n = w^* + X^{\dagger} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{E_i}{i}, \qquad X^{\dagger} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top
blocks.caption: The noise vectors E_i are independent with mean zero, so in the squared error every cross term between two different iterations averages to zero and only the squares remain: variances add. Weight 1 gives n copies of the one-fit error; weight 1/i gives the sum of 1/i^2.

blocks.md: That is the key difference from replace. The errors of different iterations neither cancel (they are independent, not opposite) nor compound multiplicatively (the fit is linear in the labels and every iteration reuses the same inputs $X$): they add like the steps of a random walk. Replace adds a full step every iteration, so the error grows linearly. Accumulate adds steps of shrinking size $1/i$, whose squares $1/i^2$ sum to at most $\pi^2/6 \approx 1.645$, so the total error is bounded no matter how many iterations run.

blocks.prompt: Take $d = 10$ features, $T = 100$ samples per iteration, $\sigma^2 = 1$. The prefactor is $10/89 = 0.1124$. Predict the test error after 10 iterations under each strategy.
blocks.reveal: **Replace: 1.124**, ten times the first model's error. **Accumulate: 0.174**, since $\sum_{i=1}^{10} 1/i^2 = 1.550$, and it can never exceed $0.1124 \times 1.645 = 0.185$. A 4,000-run simulation of exactly this setup gave 1.108 and 0.172.

blocks.title: Linear regression test error: replace vs accumulate (d = 10, T = 100)

scenes.caption: Iteration 1: both strategies have seen only real data, so both errors are 0.112.
Iteration 2: replace doubles to 0.225; accumulate rises only to 0.140, since the new synthetic labels are half the training set.
Iteration 5: replace 0.562, accumulate 0.165. Each new accumulated batch matters less than the one before.
Iteration 10: replace 1.124 and still growing linearly; accumulate 0.174, under the 0.185 bound it can never cross.

blocks.md: Their language-model experiments agreed: GPT-2 and Llama-2 style models from 9M to about 125M parameters, pretrained from scratch on TinyStories (short children's stories written by GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 using words a young child knows) for five iterations, showed rising test loss under replace and flat loss under accumulate. Related theory points the same way. Bertrand et al. prove iterative retraining is stable if the first model is close enough to the data and the share of clean data is large enough. Dohmatob et al. show that mixing even a small fraction of real data eventually ends the scaling plateau of lesson 3.

Mixing helps, but how much synthetic data is too much? A later paper from the same group, *Strong Model Collapse* (Dohmatob, Feng, Subramonian and Kempe, 2024), studies a fixed share $p_2$ of synthetic data in a growing training set of $n$ samples (here $n$ counts samples, not iterations). In their linear regression model, the synthetic labels come from a slightly wrong weight vector, offset from the true one by a random amount whose size $c^2$ measures the quality of the synthetic data (0 is perfect). For small $d/n$ their Corollary 1 gives the test error below: the first term is ordinary scaling, the second a floor that more data never removes unless the synthetic share goes to zero. This is the sense of their headline that as little as 1% synthetic data can lead to collapse: larger training sets stop improving the model. Real data rescued the tail-cut model of lesson 3 because its synthetic data were correct but incomplete; here they are systematically wrong, and a fixed share of wrong labels biases the fit however much real data sit beside it.

blocks.caption: n is the total number of samples (real plus synthetic), p2 the synthetic share, c^2 the mismatch between the synthetic and real labelling functions. In words: error is the usual sigma^2 d over n, plus p2 squared times c^2.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d, sigma, c2 = 10, 1.0, 1.0

def test_error(n, p2, reps=20):
    errs = []
    for _ in range(reps):
        w1 = rng.normal(size=d) / np.sqrt(d)                 # true weights
        w2 = w1 + rng.normal(size=d) * np.sqrt(c2 / d)       # synthetic source
        n2 = int(p2 * n); n1 = n - n2
        X = rng.normal(size=(n, d))
        w = np.r_[np.tile(w1, (n1, 1)), np.tile(w2, (n2, 1))]
        y = (X * w).sum(1) + sigma * rng.normal(size=n)
        w_hat = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
        errs.append(np.sum((w_hat - w1) ** 2))               # test MSE, Sigma = I
    return np.mean(errs)

for p2 in (0.0, 0.01, 0.1):
    row = [test_error(n, p2) for n in (10**3, 10**4, 10**5, 10**6)]
    print(f"p2={p2:4}: " + "  ".join(f"{e:.2e}" for e in row),
          f"| floor p2^2 c^2 = {p2**2 * c2:.0e}")
print("real-data law sigma^2 d/n:", "  ".join(f"{sigma**2*d/n:.2e}" for n in (10**3,10**4,10**5,10**6)))

blocks.title: Strong model collapse: a fixed synthetic share floors the error

scenes.caption: Real data only (d = 10, noise variance 1): error is d/n, falling tenfold per tenfold more data.
1% synthetic with c^2 = 1: the floor is 0.0001. The simulation matches real-only scaling up to about n = 10^4, then flattens: 0.000094 at n = 10^6, nine times the real-only error.

10% synthetic: the floor is 0.01 and already dominates at n = 10^4. From 10^5 to 10^6 samples the error barely moves (0.0103 to 0.0099). Simplified: one-shot mixing in linear regression, no feedback loop.

blocks.md: Accumulation is not a free pass. The bound depends on the original real data never being thrown away, and on synthetic data being added on top rather than diluting a fixed budget: a variant that trains on n times more pure synthetic data still diverges, only more slowly (logarithmically). MAD also reports that a fixed real set only delayed degradation in its image experiments.

Do these results contradict each other? Mostly they answer different questions. Schaeffer et al. (*Position: Model Collapse Does Not Mean What You Think*, 2025) hand-annotated 28 papers and found **eight definitions** of model collapse in three families: how test loss on real data behaves over iterations (any increase, a catastrophic increase, or divergence to infinity), how the distribution deforms (collapsing variance, lost or merged modes, vanishing tails, hallucinated data), and a **change in the scaling law**. Replace loops (lessons 1, 2 and 4, and the replace regression above) show divergence and vanishing tails. Accumulation keeps the error bounded, yet still above what the same amount of real data would give. Strong model collapse is a scaling-law change: error stops falling but does not explode. Schaeffer et al. argue realistic pretraining keeps real data and accumulates synthetic data alongside it, which avoids divergence, while loss of tail data remains a real concern.

The question is not whether synthetic data enter the loop, but whether real data stay in it. Keep the original human data, keep adding fresh real data, and treat synthetic data as an addition. Even then, a fixed share of mismatched synthetic data floors the error, so its quality matters as much as its quantity.

blocks.question: Under accumulation with d = 10, T = 100 and noise variance 1, what is the test error after iteration 2?
options: 0.225, twice the first iteration
0.112, unchanged
0.185, the bound
0.140, which is 1.25 times the first iteration
blocks.explain: The sum is 1 + 1/4 = 1.25, so the error is 0.1124 x 1.25 = 0.140. Doubling (0.225) is the replace result.

blocks.question: A lab plans each new model's pretraining mix with a fixed 10-trillion-token budget: every year it removes old human text to make room for the latest scrape, which is increasingly model-written. Which strategy from this lesson does that resemble most?
options: Accumulate, because the dataset is being refreshed
Replace, because older real data are discarded and model output takes their place
The fresh data loop, which MAD found safe in all cases
None, because a 10-trillion-token budget is too large for collapse
blocks.explain: Holding the budget fixed while swapping out human text for model output drifts toward the replace setting, where errors compound. Keeping the original real data and growing the corpus matches the accumulate results.

blocks.question: A lab keeps all its human text and, every year, adds model-written text so that a steady 20% of the mix is synthetic, from generators whose outputs differ systematically from human text. It then scales the total data tenfold. Which prediction fits the results in this lesson best?
options: Test error diverges, as in the replace loop
Test error keeps falling as a power law, because real data are never thrown away
The model collapses to a point mass within a few generations
Test error stops improving at a floor set by the synthetic share and its mismatch, but does not diverge
blocks.explain: Real data are kept, so this is not the replace setting and nothing diverges. But a fixed, non-vanishing share of mismatched data adds a floor of about p2^2 c^2 (strong model collapse): a change in the scaling law, which is one of the eight definitions Schaeffer et al. list.

lessons.title: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor

blocks.md: Collapse results describe uncurated loops where a model swallows its own unfiltered output. Successful synthetic data pipelines look different in three ways: they **filter** outputs using a signal that does not come from the generator alone, they **inject diversity** on purpose, and they keep **real data** in the mix. Three well-known papers show each piece.

**Self-Instruct** (Wang et al.) bootstrapped instruction-tuning data from vanilla GPT-3 (the original pretrained model, with no instruction tuning). Starting from 175 human-written seed tasks, the model generates new instructions, inputs and outputs. A new instruction is kept only if its ROUGE-L similarity (the longest-common-subsequence score from lesson 4) to every instruction already in the pool is below 0.7. Invalid ones and ones that fail this check are removed.

The run produced about 52K instructions with about 82K instances (an instance is one input and output example for an instruction), and fine-tuning GPT-3 on them gave a 33% absolute improvement on Super-NaturalInstructions (a benchmark of over 1,600 language tasks, each with expert-written instructions; Self-Instruct was scored on its held-out tasks), on par with InstructGPT-001.

blocks.title: A novelty filter in the style of Self-Instruct (simplified)

scenes.caption: ROUGE-L F1 is based on the longest common subsequence of words: 2 x LCS divided by the total length of both instructions.
A near-duplicate: 5 of its 6 words appear in order in a pool instruction, so the score is 10/11 = 0.91. Rejected.
scenes.output: Write a short poem about rain 0.91 2

Sort a list of numbers in reverse 0.83 3

blocks.md: **phi-1** (Gunasekar et al., *Textbooks Are All You Need*) is a 1.3B-parameter code model trained on about 6B tokens of web code filtered for "educational value" (a classifier trained on GPT-4 annotations), under 1B tokens of GPT-3.5-generated Python textbooks, and about 180M tokens of synthetic exercises for fine-tuning. It reached 50.6% **pass@1** (the share of problems where the model's first generated solution passes all the unit tests) on HumanEval (164 hand-written Python programming problems with unit tests, from OpenAI) and 55.5% on MBPP (Mostly Basic Python Problems, about 1,000 entry-level Python tasks, from Google). The authors stress that naive prompting gives "homogeneous and redundant" data, so they forced diversity by constraining the topics and target audience of each generated textbook.

**STaR** (Zelikman et al., *Self-Taught Reasoner*) makes a model write step-by-step rationales for questions, keeps only rationales that reach the correct answer, retries with the answer given as a hint when it fails, fine-tunes on the kept rationales, and repeats. The filter is a ground-truth label, a signal from outside the model, which is what the uncurated loops in lessons 1 to 5 lacked.

blocks.title: Anatomy of a synthetic data pipeline

scenes.caption: Diversity is injected at the input: varied seeds, topics, audiences or random constraints, because a generator left alone follows its most probable paths.
The filter uses signals the generator does not control: correct answers (STaR), unit tests, a quality classifier (phi-1), or novelty checks (Self-Instruct).
Kept samples join real data rather than replacing it, which is the accumulate setting of lesson 5.
Evaluate on held-out real data, not on synthetic data: a collapsed model can look excellent on its own outputs while losing the tails.

blocks.md: Things to monitor in any synthetic data loop: the diversity metrics of lesson 4 on the generated set (distinct-n, self-ROUGE-L or Self-BLEU, embedding spread), performance on rare slices of a real held-out set, and the share of real data in the mix.

Anchoring on real data assumes you can tell real data from model output. Shumailov et al. argue that access to the original data source must be preserved, that data about genuine human interactions become more valuable, and that without **provenance** (a record of where each document came from) it may become hard to train new models without data crawled before the mass adoption of LLMs. Three practical options:

1. **A protected anchor**: keep pre-LLM snapshots and sources known to be human, and never drop them (the accumulate setting of lesson 5).
2. **Classifier filtering** of model-written text in new crawls.
3. **Watermarking**: generators plant a hidden statistical signal in their output; it only marks text from generators that cooperate.

Detection has hard limits. Sadasivan et al. (*Can AI-Generated Text be Reliably Detected?*) show that recursive paraphrasing, rewriting a text several times with another model, sharply cuts the detection rate of watermark-based, neural, zero-shot and retrieval-based detectors while degrading quality only slightly. They also bound the **AUROC** of the best possible detector (the area under the ROC curve: the chance that a random AI text scores above a random human text, 0.5 being a coin flip) by the **total variation distance** between human and AI text, the largest difference in probability the two distributions give to any set of texts. As models write more like humans that distance shrinks. So filtering is a useful extra, while keeping and growing known-human data is the dependable defense.
Synthetic data are useful when an outside signal decides what is kept, diversity is designed in, and real data stay in the training mix. Model collapse is what happens when all three are missing.

blocks.question: A team fine-tunes a model on its own sampled answers to math problems, sampled at temperature 0.3, keeping all of them, for five rounds. Accuracy on their synthetic validation set rises but falls on real exam questions. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The learning rate was too high
No outside signal filters the answers and low temperature narrows the outputs, so each round reinforces the model's own errors and loses rare solution paths
Five rounds is too few for self-training to converge
Math problems cannot benefit from synthetic data
blocks.explain: This is a closed, replacing, tail-cutting loop. STaR-style filtering by correct answers, higher-diversity sampling, and keeping real data in the mix address each part. Validating on synthetic data hid the damage.

blocks.question: Which change most directly addresses the failure that phi-1's authors warned about when prompting a model to write textbooks?
options: Lower the sampling temperature for cleaner text
Generate ten times more textbooks from the same prompt
Vary the topic and target audience in each generation prompt
Train the student for more epochs on the synthetic set
blocks.explain: Their concern was homogeneous, redundant output: a generator repeats its most probable content. Constraining topics and audiences forces coverage. Lower temperature and more samples from one prompt make redundancy worse.

blocks.question: A lab wants its 2027 pretraining mix to stay anchored to human text. Which plan does this lesson support best?
options: Keep pre-LLM snapshots and other known-human sources permanently in the mix, and treat classifier or watermark filtering of new crawls as an extra layer
Rely on an AI-text classifier to remove all model-written pages from new crawls, then drop the old snapshots to save space
Rely on watermarks, since every model that writes web text embeds one
Ignore provenance, since accumulating any data at all prevents every form of collapse
blocks.explain: Detectors can be evaded by paraphrasing and are bounded by how close AI text is to human text, and watermarks cover only cooperating generators. Known-human data kept permanently is the anchor that does not depend on detection. Accumulation bounds error but does not by itself protect the tails.

lessons.title: Verification is the fix: why filtered self-training does not collapse

blocks.md: Start small. A model answers 100 questions and gets 60 right. Train on all 100 answers and 40% of the lessons are wrong. Now add a checker that keeps a right answer 90% of the time and a wrong one only 20% of the time. It keeps 54 right and 8 wrong answers: a set of 62 that is 87% right. The generator did not improve; the **selection** did. Lesson 6 claimed that an outside filter separates working pipelines from collapse. This lesson makes that precise.

Feng et al. (*Beyond Model Collapse: Scaling Up with Synthesized Data Requires Verification*, 2024) first show that the good answers are often already there. A transformer trained to predict eigenvalues of 5 by 5 matrices was asked for 50 candidate answers with beam search. At 1% tolerance, the best of the 50 was correct 60.4% of the time, but the candidate the model itself ranked best by perplexity only 19.2%, about three times worse. The model can generate good answers; it cannot pick them.

Their theory names the pieces. The generator is wrong with probability $p$. A **verifier** (any selector: a checker, another model, a human) keeps a correct example with probability $\phi$, its true positive rate, and a wrong one with probability $\psi$, its false positive rate. No filter is $\phi = \psi = 1$; an oracle that knows the truth is $\phi = 1, \psi = 0$. Training a linear classifier on the kept synthetic data in the limit of infinite data, Theorem 4.2 finds a sharp **breakdown point** $p^*$: below it the trained model reaches the best possible (Bayes-optimal) accuracy, above it the model learns the exact opposite of the true labels.

blocks.tex: \text{kept accuracy} = \frac{(1-p)\,\phi}{(1-p)\,\phi + p\,\psi}, \qquad p^* = \frac{1}{1 + \psi/\phi}, \qquad p < p^* \iff (1-p)\,\phi > p\,\psi
blocks.caption: The condition p < p* is the same as saying the kept set is mostly right: more correct examples survive than wrong ones. With no filter p* = 1/2; with phi = 0.9 and psi = 0.2, p* = 0.82.

blocks.title: Accuracy of the kept set: generator accuracy in, filtered accuracy out

y.label: accuracy of the kept synthetic set

scenes.caption: No filter (phi = psi = 1): the kept set is exactly as accurate as the generator. Breakdown at 50%: a generator wrong more often than right teaches the opposite.
Verifier with phi = 0.9, psi = 0.2: a 60% generator becomes an 87% kept set, and breakdown moves down to 18% generator accuracy (p* = 0.82).
A near-oracle (phi = 1, psi = 0.05): almost any generator that is sometimes right yields a clean kept set. Breakdown is at about 5% accuracy.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d = 50
w_true = rng.normal(size=d); w_true /= np.linalg.norm(w_true)

def data(n):                      # two Gaussian classes at +-0.15 w_true
    y = rng.choice([-1, 1], n)
    x = 0.15 * y[:, None] * w_true + rng.normal(size=(n, d)) / np.sqrt(d)
    return x, y

def experiment(p, phi, psi, n):
    x, y = data(n)
    y_syn = np.where(rng.random(n) < p, -y, y)          # generator: wrong w.p. p
    right = y_syn == y
    keep = np.where(right, rng.random(n) < phi, rng.random(n) < psi)
    w = np.linalg.lstsq(x[keep], y_syn[keep], rcond=None)[0]
    xt, _ = data(20000)
    agree = np.mean(np.sign(xt @ w) == np.sign(xt @ w_true))  # vs Bayes rule
    return right[keep].mean(), agree

for p, phi, psi, name in [(0.4, 1, 1, "no filter"), (0.4, 0.9, 0.2, "verifier"),
                          (0.6, 1, 1, "no filter"), (0.6, 0.9, 0.2, "verifier"),
                          (0.4, 1, 0, "oracle")]:
    pstar = 1 / (1 + psi / phi)
    cells = [experiment(p, phi, psi, n) for n in (1000, 10000, 100000)]
    print(f"gen acc {1-p:.0%} {name:9s} p*={pstar:.2f} kept acc {cells[-1][0]:.2f} "
          "| match Bayes at n=1e3,1e4,1e5: " + " ".join(f"{a:.2f}" for _, a in cells))
blocks.caption:
Real output, agreement with the best classifier at n = 10^3, 10^4, 10^5:
60% no filter (kept 0.60): 0.71 0.89 0.96
60% verifier (kept 0.87): 0.87 0.96 0.99
40% no filter (kept 0.40): 0.32 0.12 0.04
40% verifier (kept 0.75): 0.78 0.94 0.98
60% oracle (kept 1.00): 0.91 0.98 0.99

blocks.md: The phase transition shows up in a tiny CPU run. A 40%-accurate generator without a filter is past the breakdown point: as $n$ grows the model agrees with the best classifier less and less (0.32, 0.12, 0.04), converging on the opposite rule. The same generator behind the verifier rises to 0.98. Even below breakdown, the filter helps at finite data: 0.87 against 0.71 at $n = 1000$. Simplified: here errors are random label flips, matching the theory's assumption that each example's fate is independent. Real generator errors are systematic, which is why in Feng et al.'s eigenvalue experiment, training on 10 million unverified examples (50 times the generator's own training set) still did worse than the generator itself, while verified data nearly doubled accuracy with the oracle.

blocks.prompt: In Feng et al.'s news summarization experiment, Llama-2-7B writes the summaries. To select which to train on, is it better to have the stronger Llama-3 pick the summaries it finds most likely, or Llama-2 pick its own most likely ones?
blocks.reveal: Surprisingly, **self-selection by Llama-2 was better**; selection by Llama-3 performed about like random selection. The measured $p^*$ explained it: a verifier helps only if its judgments line up with which of *this* generator's outputs are good, and a stronger model is not automatically that. Selection with the oracle (the human reference summaries) did best: keeping only 12.5% of the synthetic summaries beat a model trained on 100% of the original human labels.

blocks.md: Labs use exactly this pattern. **ReST** (Reinforced Self-Training, Gulcehre et al., Google DeepMind, 2023) alternates two steps. **Grow**: the current model samples many outputs per input and a learned reward model scores each. **Improve**: fine-tune on samples whose reward exceeds a threshold $\tau$, then raise $\tau$ and repeat on the same Grow data. The original dataset stays in the training mix "to ensure that the policies do not diverge": verification and a real anchor together.

blocks.title: ReST: Grow once, Improve with a rising threshold

scenes.caption: Grow: the current policy samples many outputs per input, and a learned reward model scores every one. In the paper the task is machine translation.
An Improve step: only samples with reward above the threshold are kept, and the original data D stay in the mix so the policy does not diverge.
Later Improve steps reuse the same Grow data with a higher threshold, so each step trains on a smaller, better subset. The paper used thresholds 0.0, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99.
The improved policy then runs a new Grow step. Human raters preferred one Grow step even though reward kept rising: the reward model is only a proxy.

blocks.md: **Rejection sampling fine-tuning**, which you met in the *How LLMs are trained* course (Llama 2 used it), is the same idea at scale: sample several answers, keep the one a scorer prefers, and fine-tune on the kept ones. In Llama 3 post-training (Meta, 2024), for each prompt the team sampled $K$ outputs, typically 10 to 30, from the latest chat model and let a reward model pick the best for the next round of fine-tuning. For code, they report that training the 405B model on its own generated data was not helpful and could even degrade performance, so they added execution feedback as a source of truth: a parser and linter, model-written unit tests run in a container, and failed solutions sent back for revision. The pipeline produced about one million synthetic coding dialogues, and only dialogues passing every check went into fine-tuning; about 20% of solutions were initially wrong and then self-corrected. For math, traces were filtered by the correct answer and by outcome and stepwise reward models.

The generator does not have to be right; the kept set has to be. Collapse is avoided when a verifier keeps more correct than incorrect examples, and its judgments must track this generator's actual errors.

A learned reward model is itself a model, and optimizing against it can exploit its blind spots. In ReST, human raters preferred models from a single Grow step even though reward-model scores kept rising with more steps. Programmatic checks (tests, exact answers) are sturdier, as in Llama 3's execution feedback above.

blocks.question: A generator is right 50% of the time. A verifier keeps 80% of correct examples and 40% of wrong ones. What is the accuracy of the kept set, and is the generator below the breakdown point?
options: About 67%, and yes: p = 0.5 is below p* = 0.67
50%, since a filter cannot add correct examples
About 80%, the verifier's true positive rate
About 67%, but no: any generator that is wrong half the time is past breakdown
blocks.explain: Kept right: 0.5 x 0.8 = 0.40; kept wrong: 0.5 x 0.4 = 0.20; accuracy 0.40/0.60 = 0.67. The breakdown point is 1/(1 + 0.4/0.8) = 0.67, and p = 0.5 is below it, so the kept set is mostly right. Without the filter p* is 0.5 and this generator would sit exactly on the edge.

blocks.question: Recall the team in lesson 6 that fine-tuned on all its own temperature-0.3 math answers for five rounds and watched real exam accuracy fall. Which single change turns their loop into the verified pattern of this lesson?
options: Train more epochs per round so the model fits its answers better
Ask a larger model to pick the answers it likes best, without checking how well its choices track correctness
Sample many answers per problem and keep only those whose final answer matches the known solution, as in STaR and Llama 3
Lower the temperature further so answers are more consistent
blocks.explain: A ground-truth check is a verifier with very low psi, which pushes the breakdown point toward 1. A stronger judge helps only if its choices track the generator's actual errors (the Llama-3 surprise above), and more epochs or lower temperature narrow the outputs further.

lessons.title: Synthetic data at scale: rephrasing, textbooks, reward-filtered SFT

blocks.md: Lesson 6's examples were small: 52K instructions, under a billion tokens of textbooks. Today synthetic data also shape pretraining mixes of billions of tokens and nearly all of some alignment datasets. Three published pipelines show how, and each leans on one of lesson 6's three ingredients more than the others: an outside filter, injected diversity, or a real-data anchor.

**WRAP** (Web Rephrase Augmented Pretraining, Maini et al., 2024) uses a frozen Mistral-7B instruction model to paraphrase documents from C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus), a large cleaned web crawl, in four styles: Easy ("text that even a toddler will understand"), Medium ("high quality English such as that found on Wikipedia"), Hard (terse, abstruse), and Q/A (conversational question and answer). Chunks are capped at 300 tokens, since longer rephrasings often lost information. Real and synthetic text are sampled 1:1. Reported results: about 3 times faster pretraining; at the same compute, perplexity more than 10% lower on average across subsets of the Pile, a diverse evaluation corpus; and over 2% higher zero-shot accuracy on 13 question-answering tasks.

The real half matters. Training on rephrased text alone raised perplexity on domains such as Philpapers and Gutenberg; the authors attribute this to synthetic text lacking the tags and styles that real web text has. WRAP never asks the model for new knowledge: every fact comes from a real document, and the generator only changes the style. That is the real-data anchor taken to its limit.

**Cosmopedia** (Hugging Face, 2024) set out to reproduce the synthetic textbooks behind Microsoft's Phi models in the open: over 30 million files and 25 billion tokens of textbooks, blog posts, stories and WikiHow-style articles from Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct, over 10k GPU hours. The hard part was diversity. Prompts came from curated sources (Stanford course outlines, Khan Academy, OpenStax, WikiHow) and, for over 80% of them, from web samples clustered into 145 topics, 112 of which were kept. Each topic was rewritten for 4 audiences (young children, high school, college, researchers) and 3 styles. The authors report under 1% duplicate content. They also found the model reusing openings such as "Once upon a time" and prompted it to avoid them.

A generator can also reproduce test questions it saw in training or in its seeds, which inflates benchmark scores; this is **contamination**. Cosmopedia's check, following phi-1: find samples sharing a 10-word run with a benchmark item, then discard those whose matched text covers more than half of the item. Liu et al. (*Best Practices and Lessons Learned on Synthetic Data*, 2024) warn that synthetic data can contain *rephrased* benchmark items, which such token-level checks miss, and recommend protected in-house evaluation sets.

blocks.title: Benchmark decontamination in the style of Cosmopedia (simplified)

scenes.caption: Step 1 finds candidates cheaply: does the sample share any run of 10 consecutive words with a benchmark item?
Step 2 confirms with difflib's SequenceMatcher: the matched characters as a share of the benchmark item. Above 0.5, the sample is discarded.
A textbook page that pasted the benchmark question verbatim: it shares 10-grams and matches 100% of the item. Discarded.
The same question reworded by a generator shares no 10-gram, so it is never even compared. Token-level checks miss paraphrased test items.

blocks.md: **Nemotron-4 340B** (NVIDIA, 2024) is the alignment end of the spectrum. The team used only about 20K human-annotated examples (10K for supervised fine-tuning, 10K HelpSteer2 preference pairs for the reward model), while over 98% of the fine-tuning and preference data was synthetic. Prompts were generated by Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct from about 3K topics (and from C4 documents for closed questions), with task, topic and format varied on purpose. Responses were scored by Nemotron-4-340B-Reward and those below a threshold dropped. For preference pairs, answers to math training problems were judged against ground truth and instruction-following answers by Python checkers; elsewhere the reward model judged, since on the hard chat category of RewardBench (a benchmark of preference pairs for testing reward models) it was right 0.87 of the time against 0.54 for an LLM judge.

blocks.title: Three production pipelines, same three ingredients

scenes.caption: WRAP: Mistral-7B rephrases real C4 documents into four styles, and real and rephrased text are mixed 1:1. The knowledge comes from the real documents; the real half keeps the noise and styles of the web.

Cosmopedia: over 30 million prompts built from curricula and clustered web samples, varied by 4 audiences and 3 styles, fed to Mixtral-8x7B. Diversity is engineered into the prompts; outputs are decontaminated against benchmarks.

scenes.caption: Nemotron-4 340B alignment: synthetic prompts from 3K topics and C4 documents, responses from the current best model, scored by a reward model trained on 10K human preferences or checked against ground truth. About 20K human examples sit alongside.

blocks.prompt: Nemotron's first generator was Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct; its data trained an intermediate 340B model, which then generated data for the next round. Can a student trained on a weaker teacher's filtered data end up stronger than that teacher?
blocks.reveal: **Yes.** The report says the teacher "does not impose a ceiling": the first 340B intermediate instruct model surpassed Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct, and became the generator for round two, which they call iterative weak-to-strong alignment. Contrast Llama 3, where the 405B model trained on its own unchecked code was not helped. The difference is what sits between generator and student: a stronger base model plus a reward model and ground-truth checks anchored in human data. Nor does over 98% synthetic contradict lesson 5's strong model collapse: that floor grows with the mismatch $c^2$ between synthetic and true labels, and this filtering is what keeps the mismatch small.

blocks.md: At scale the recipe is the same as at small scale. Knowledge or judgment must come from outside the generator: real documents to rephrase (WRAP), real seeds and engineered variety (Cosmopedia), or a filter trained on human preferences and ground truth (Nemotron). Decontaminate against your evaluations.

blocks.question: Which ingredient does WRAP depend on most, judging by its own ablation?
options: A reward model that filters rephrasings
Real web documents: they supply every fact, and dropping the real half of the mix hurt perplexity on several domains
Benchmark-style prompts that inject topics the web lacks
Recursive self-training, where each model rephrases for the next
blocks.explain: WRAP has no filtering stage and no new topics; the generator only restyles real C4 text, and the 1:1 real share was needed for domains with web-specific styles. It is a real-data anchor plus style diversity.

blocks.question: A synthetic textbook includes a reworded version of a test question from MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding, a 57-subject benchmark). Your decontamination uses 10-gram overlap followed by a SequenceMatcher check. What happens, and what is the sturdier defense?
options: It is caught, because SequenceMatcher compares every sample with every benchmark item
It is caught, because rewording keeps most 10-word runs intact
It does not matter, since contamination only affects pretraining data, not synthetic data
It slips through, since no 10-word run is shared; keep a protected in-house evaluation set the generator never saw
blocks.explain: The 10-gram step decides which samples are compared at all, so a paraphrase with no shared 10-gram is never checked. Liu et al. note exactly this gap and recommend safeguarded private benchmarks.
